W1-1.note: Grandfather says outright, "I marked that bevel wrong," and then re-measures every frame.

W1-2.note: Ada's steam log shows she pulled the plank after forty minutes instead of an hour, and the frames all turn out to match the plans.

W1-3.note: The paragraph is about Corran's visit and his offer to finish the Linnet in his yard.

W1-4.note: "A fair distance up the coast" means a sizable distance, which is why Ada had time to hurry the plank.

W1-5.note: She watches him fumble the latch and counts the months to June over and over, which suggests she doubts his hands will last until next summer; "wistful" can also be defended.

W1-6.note: Grandfather says the two of them will rebuild the Linnet properly next summer and skip the regatta.

W2-1.note: He tested a bell against heavy surf while Lise marked where each stroke was drowned out, which shows he blamed a bell that could not be heard over the surf.

W2-2.note: The board ordered a heavier bell, and it went up in 1872.

W2-3.note: The logbook marks each stroke until dawn, which shows Holm rang the bell all night.

W2-4.note: Coming down the coast "on a fair wind" means a favorable wind.

W2-5.note: The board acted "on the keeper's account of the night" after Reddick praised Holm's knowledge, though its tight budget also played a part.

W2-6.note: The author dwells on Holm's all-night bell, his surf tests and eighteen years without a wreck, which reads as admiration; "sympathetic" is close.
